title: ATO 2026: Open Source Licensing 101
content:
In October, the OSI hosted the State of the Source track at All Things Open designed to connect developers with the big policy conversations shaping our ecosystem. McCoy Smith, Chair of OSI’s License Committee, presented “Open Source Licensing 101.”

This essential session is a basic primer on what the Open Source Initiative is, the Open Source licenses they approve, and the broader categories those license fall into. Also included are tips for understanding the OSI license approval process and the Open Source Definition and Open Source AI Definition. An overview of some of the more prominent approved Open Source licenses was provided. Other related topics like best practices, available resources and other information for working best within Open Source was also provided.

  • What is Copyright
  • What is a Patent
  • What is a License
  • What is Copyleft
  • What is Dual Licensing
  • How to Choose a License
  • Releasing Open Source Software

title: ATO 2026: The State of the Open Source Initiative
content:
In October, the OSI hosted the State of the Source track at All Things Open designed to connect developers with the big policy conversations shaping our ecosystem. Duane O’Brien, Executive Director of the OSI, opened the track with “The State of the Open Source Initiative.”

2026 has been an important year of transition for the Open Source Initiative, with a new Executive Director and multiple initiatives across Licensing, Policy, Standards, Open Source AI, and more. Duane O’Brien presented an overview of the OSI’s plans for 2027, and a readout on our mission, vision, and programs.

title: ATO 2026: Sharing is caring – Open data for Open Source compliance
content:
In October, the OSI hosted the State of the Source track at All Things Open designed to connect developers with the big policy conversations shaping our ecosystem. Nick Vidal and Brian Duran, members of the ClearlyDefined Outreach Committee, presented “Sharing is caring: Open data for Open Source compliance.”

Open Source compliance depends on accurate data about millions of software components, yet organizations often duplicate efforts and build isolated datasets. ClearlyDefined offers a better approach: shared, community-verified open data on software component provenance, license, and vulnerabilities that improves accuracy, reduces duplication, and enables compliance automation at scale.

Nick Vidal: Hello. Good morning, everyone. We’re going to be continuing the conversation. McCoy gave a great presentation around open source licensing, and now we’re going to be getting into compliance. We want to present a really interesting project called ClearlyDefined. The idea behind ClearlyDefined is sharing license data. Let’s first start with who we are.

My name is Nick Vidal. I work with the OSI. I’m a community manager, and this is my colleague Brian.

title: Open Source AI Salons and What’s Next
content:
Dear OSI community,

The fall conference season in the US is especially busy. I’ve been fortunate enough to attend several events in the last month, but it was especially great to reconnect with the community at All Things Open. This was my first big Open Source conference as Executive Director as we hosted the State of the Source track. Many of our sessions were standing room only, and the feedback we heard was generous and useful. We’re grateful for that, and we’ll be posting recordings of the sessions soon.

The day after All Things Open, we hosted our first Open Source AI Salon. This was an important moment for us as we re-engage the community to discuss the Open Source AI Definition, look at everything we’ve collectively learned since version 1.0 was published two years ago, and chart the course for our next steps. We’ll be hosting many more of these events in the coming months. Watch this space for details.
creator: Nick Vidal

title: Open Source AI Salons: Shaping the OSAID, Together
content:
Two years after the release of the Open Source AI Definition (OSAID 1.0), the Open Source Initiative hosted the first in a series of Open Source AI Salons, gatherings to discuss the future of the OSAID. In collaboration with key partners in Raleigh and Barcelona, the events brought together civil society, government, industry, and academia to understand the practical application of the OSAID.

These interdisciplinary, community-driven events provide the ground to surface challenges, examine assumptions, and explore practical issues affecting the Open Source community when it comes to AI. As we head into 2027, we are developing opportunities to bring candid discussions about the OSAID to more people in more places. OSI is steadfast in its commitment to empowering the Open Source community and promoting a healthy Open Source AI ecosystem.

title: FOSDEM 2027: CFP for Open Source & EU Policy Devroom
content:
The Open Source Initiative, in collaboration with APELL, Eclipse Foundation, Github, Linux Foundation Europe, Mozilla, NLNET Labs, Open Forum Europe, OpenSSF, and Red Hat are delighted to invite you to submit a proposal for a talk, and join us for the 4th edition of the Open Source & EU Policy devroom at FOSDEM on Sunday, January 31st 2027, to explore how FLOSS interacts with the EU, including how ongoing and upcoming EU laws could impact the FLOSS ecosystem, what we have to gain, what we have to lose, and what needs to change.

The devroom will focus on bringing together FLOSS communities and EU lawmakers, including Members of the European Parliament, and Staff from the Parliament and the Commission, helping lawmakers improve their laws and address major challenges, such as digital sovereignty and secure, interoperable technology; while giving FLOSS communities and the Digital Commons a place to raise concerns, propose improvements and changes, and figure out how best to prepare for and respond to policy proposals.

title: Opening New Paths for Open Source
content:
Dear OSI community,

The past few weeks took me from New York to Halifax to Prague, and I came home with a full notebook and a long list of follow-ups.

At UN Digital Cooperation Day (part of the 81st UN General Assembly), I joined a panel on Open Source AI to reinforce the importance of shared language and common definitions when crafting policy. Later that day I joined Creative Commons and the NYU Engelberg Center for a conversation about openness and digital sovereignty. My key message there was simple: open by itself does very little, but enables a lot. You can read more about these talks, plus the inaugural 50-in-5 Awards, in Nick Vidal’s blog post Open Enables a Lot: The OSI at UNGA81.

My next stop was Stakeholder Day as part of Open Source Congress in Halifax. It was great to connect with leaders from more than 40 foundations as they formed working groups on global collaboration, sustainability, security, regulatory policy, AI, and governance. These are big problems, and it was encouraging to see so many organizations sign up to work on them together.

title: New website reflects OSI’s evolving mission
content:
Over the years, OSI’s work has expanded beyond the Open Source Definition and licensing to encompass policy and standards, research and education, and Open Source AI. The new website brings these areas into clearer focus, making it easier for the community and our partners to discover what we do and find ways to get involved.

The new website architecture organizes OSI’s work around its major strategic areas: Licensing, Open Source AI, Policy & Standards, Research & Education, and Community.

One of the most significant changes is elevating Policy & Standards to a primary navigation category. This will make our policy positions, regulatory engagement, and work across regions and topics easier to find.

We’re also expanding the visibility of Research & Education initiatives, including our work with the Open Technology Research (OTR) Network and the development of the Open Source Licensing Education hub.

Finally, under Community, we are creating dedicated pathways for different audiences, including maintainers and developers, lawyers and legal professionals, founders and executives, nonprofits and academia, and policymakers and government.

title: Announcing the 2027 State of Open Source Survey
content:
The Open Source Initiative (OSI) has teamed up again with Perforce Zend and OpenLogic, as well as the Eclipse Foundation, for the 2027 State of Open Source Survey.

This annual survey, now in its sixth year, brings together perspectives from OSS developers, administrators, and IT leaders around the world. It examines what technologies organizations are deploying, where teams are investing, and what challenges they’re facing. In 2027, that includes taking a closer look at AI, with questions covering adoption, development priorities, and how organizations are responding to a rapidly evolving regulatory environment and increased scrutiny.

The 2026 State of Open Source Survey showed how firmly open source has become established within organizational technology stacks:

  • 98% of respondents said their organizations had either increased or maintained their use of open source software over the previous year, up from 96% in 2025.
  • Avoiding vendor lock-in was cited as the most common driver of adoption, particularly for European OSS users.

title: Open Enables a Lot: The OSI at UNGA81
content:
On Monday, September 21, with the high-level week of the 81st UN General Assembly (UNGA81) underway in New York, OSI Executive Director Duane O’Brien spoke on a UN panel about Open Source AI and joined a Creative Commons symposium on openness and digital sovereignty. The OSI also attended the inaugural 50-in-5 Awards for digital public infrastructure. Different people filled each room, but many of them were circling the same question: what does openness give people, and what does it take to make good on it?

At the Creative Commons event, Duane offered a ten-word answer: “Open by itself does very little but enables a lot.” Creative Commons later called it the line of the day. Most of what the OSI said at UNGA81 was about the distance between the two halves of that sentence.

At UN Digital Cooperation Day, organized by the UN Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies (ODET), Duane joined the panel “What is Open Source AI? Applications, Strategies and Global Cooperation.” Sarah Myers West of the AI Now Institute moderated a conversation with Duane, Kari Briski of NVIDIA, Marzieh Fadaee of Cohere Labs, Jim Zemlin of the Linux Foundation, and Rumman Chowdhury of Humane Intelligence.
